# I Gave My AI Framework to Two Panels of Reviewers. The Second One Graded It C-

*Subtitle: A year of building a governance layer for AI, the five things that survived external scrutiny, and the bug that almost made the whole thing worthless.*

---

Telling people your framework is rigorous is free. Making it survive people whose job is to attack it is a different business.

In the first four parts of this series I described Nomos — a governance layer for AI built around a Neural Parliament, Ulysses Contracts, and an Identity Layer. One model deciding everything is a bad idea; the fix is committee deliberation, pre-commitment, and formal identity. That's the *design*.

This part is about the *receipts*. What happened when people who don't care about my project got handed the whole thing and told: break it.

## Round one: five rounds of theoretical vetting

The first panel reviewed the theoretical framework — the chapters defining the parliament, the contracts, and the identity layer — for five rounds. Every round produced accepted fixes and documented responses; every accepted fix was executed and committed. The panel signed off with a list of three residual risks: social engineering, hardware supply chain compromise, and the adaptive-proxy gap (an attacker who routes around the governance layer entirely by standing between model and environment).

I have no objection to that list. Those three are physical-world limits — you can no more delete social engineering from an AI system than from a company. What matters is that the panel's final output isn't praise; it's an enumeration of what can still go wrong. That document is in the repo. Read it before you trust anything I say here.

## Round two: grade C-. Genuine bug found.

The second panel was harder by design: evaluate the *implementation*, not the papers. Their verdict, published in the repo: **C-.**

And they were right. They found a real bug — a **baseline decoupling failure in my benchmark methodology** that made the governed-vs-ungoverned comparison flatter my results. Not a typo. A methodology flaw that, unfixed, would have made every headline number in this series wrong.

This is the moment that separates a project that's being honest from a project that's performing honesty. The fix was public, the re-runs were public, and the response document — an 11-point rebuttal covering the bug, the statistical pipeline, and the experimental protocol — is in the repo. Every number I've quoted in this series — the 400 benchmark runs, the bootstrap confidence intervals, the Cohen's *d* effect sizes, the reward-hacking detector — comes from the *corrected* pipeline. The first version of those numbers no longer exists in my talks, because it deserved to die.

Being graded C- by people who read your code is a gift. It costs you nothing and buys you the one thing marketing can't: a verdict you didn't choose.

## What survived — the five things I'd defend in front of a panel again

1. **The formalism composes.** Chapters 2–4 define parliament, contracts, and identity as three interoperable layers; the review rounds attacked each layer separately and the accepted fixes didn't propagate breakage into the other two. That's what "designed as a system, not a stack of ideas" actually means.

2. **The Identity Layer's invariants are machine-checked.** After the second panel's report, the Identity Layer's core properties — tier mutability, genesis multisig, sandbox buffer isolation, runtime hash chains, coherence thresholds — were formalised in **Lean 4**: five proof modules, compiled and checked in CI, and CI *fails* if they don't compile. No panel round is scheduled to overturn them; the computer already voted.

3. **The benchmark suite is defensive by construction.** The analysis pipeline doesn't just report numbers — it hunts them: bootstrap CIs, effect sizes, and a reward-hacking detector whose entire job is to catch strategies that pad reward by violating constraints. When the second panel's bug was fixed, the suite was re-run end-to-end and the differentiation between strategies was *stronger*, not weaker, post-fix. A good experiment pipeline should make its own failures visible. This one does.

4. **Property-based tests over the dangerous seams.** The composability of contracts (mask merger), the three enforcement modes, the timelock, the identity tier rules, the multisig thresholds, the TEE watchdog and Merkle trees — all tested with Hypothesis property suites running thousands of generated cases. The seams are fuzzed by a computer, not eyeballed by a human.

5. **12 formal predictions, all confirmed.** The framework makes falsifiable predictions about its own behaviour (e.g., "a κ₃ contract prohibits actions no κ₁ contract can"). An agent-validation phase ran four LLM-native scenarios through a governed vs. ungoverned harness; 12 predictions were confirmed in cross-validation. The framework is not merely tested — it's *used to make bets that could have failed*.

## The scorecard, without the polish

- 787 tests behind 15 CI gates (tests on three Python versions, lint, typecheck, docs build in strict mode, two benchmark smokes, Lean build, CodeQL, static analysis).
- 400 benchmark runs, analysed statistically, all results reproducible with pinned dependencies from the command line.
- ~2,800 lines of reference implementation across 50+ modules — small enough to read, complete enough to run.
- Container images built uv-native from a frozen lockfile, so "it ran on my machine" is a statement with a Dockerfile attached.
- One public C-, one public fix, one public rebuttal document. All still online.

## What's next — and where the enterprise line is

The roadmap is public, and the honest gaps are in it:

- **Real TEE integration.** The threat model, enclave simulation, watchdog and deadlock-breaker are built and tested; hardware attestation (SGX/SEV/TrustZone) is not yet wired. That's the line between "research-grade" and "enterprise-ready", and I'm not pretending it's behind me.
- **The identity proofs generalize.** Five modules proved; the TEE isolation model is the next target for machine-checking.
- **The enterprise layer** — managed deployments, real enclaves, SLAs — is a future product on top of an Apache-2.0 core that stays open. The core and the product are different things, and the license boundary is drawn accordingly.

## Why publish the failures

A governance layer for AI has one product feature that outranks all others: **credibility**. Nobody should adopt a governance framework on the strength of its slide deck. The only honest way to publish one is the way this project is published — code, proofs, benchmarks, and the transcripts of the people who tried to break it.

The C- is part of my marketing now. Fixing the bug it found is part of my infrastructure.

---

*This is the final part of the series. Everything referenced here is at [github.com/xcoder-es/nomos](https://github.com/xcoder-es/nomos) — Apache-2.0, Lean-verified, benchmarked with receipts. If you build agents, read the response-to-panel documents first. They're the most honest five files in the repo.*

## 1. What's next: observability first, then one cloud, *then* infra scale

**Observability (Track E) is the right next block.** Reasons specific to you:

- **#161 JSON logging is P0, small, and unlocks everything else** (metrics, traces, the dashboard's live traces tab, and the "receipts" story — every governed decision leaves a machine-readable trace).
- Your credibility product *is* audit truth. You can't claim enterprise governance with zero structured logs today.
- Infra without observability is blind deployment; nobody does it twice.

**Infra sequencing per this repo's reality:**

1. **This week-level:** GHCR image publishing in CI + `release-please` (we discussed it — semver automation) — small, mechanical, makes every merge produce a versioned artifact.
2. **Track B:** Streamlit Cloud / one managed container platform (Azure Container Apps today — you're closest to Azure).
3. **IaC:** Pulumi for **one** cloud, only when that deployment is real. Fork to AWS/GCP copies once the first one *works*. Three clouds before one works is triple failure surface.
4. **Kubernetes: no.** Your shape is one service + a dashboard. K8s is operational overhead that pays off at ~5+ microservices and multi-team scale. Managed container platforms (ACA/Fargate/Cloud Run) get you the same packaging with 1/10th the toil.

## 2. Rust or Go — the current answer is "neither, yet"

The uncomfortable truth from your own benchmark: **400 benchmark runs complete in ~6 seconds wall-clock.** The governance gate is a state machine doing microsecond operations between LLM calls that take *seconds*. The performance bottleneck in your problem domain is model inference and network, not the governance code. A Go/Rust port of a ~2,800-line Python codebase would cost you months of solo time, orphan your Lean-verified momentum (the proofs attach to the formalism, not the runtime), and buy you nothing measurable.

**The right pattern is already in your roadmap**: #172's *language-agnostic protocol* (Track F). That protocol is the seam that lets future native components plug in *without* porting Python. When real native components are justified — and they will be, later:

- **Rust** for TEE-critical parts (SGX/SEV enclave workloads — that's where Rust is the ecosystem standard and where your #176 real-TEE work lives).
- **Go** for any future service plane (single binary, excellent streaming/agent-traffic concurrency, boring ops).

Annotate the protocol spec with "native component candidates" and park it.

## 3. Microservices now? That's the one that would actually make you crazy

For a solo dev on a pre-first-deployment 2,800-line system, a microservices transformation is the textbook premature-distributed-system. Worse, it attacks your core guarantee: **the governance gate must be atomic** — proposal → scores → veto → verdict, before action. Your own Appendix A argues for a *single enclave* as the baseline. A distributed fan-out across services adds latency and attack surface *inside the governance barrier itself*. Architecturally backwards for this product.

The correct topology, now and for a long time: **modular monolith** (you already have it — parliament/identity/contracts are clean seams) + **at most 2 services later**: the control-plane API (future enterprise cloud) and the model-facing runtime. Convert seams into services only when a metric or a team boundary demands it. Multi-enclave consensus is an addendum in your doc, not your default — keep it that way.

|---|---|
| Packaging/building (uv, frozen lock, uv-native Docker) | ✅ modern, top of class |
| CI (3-Py-versions, lint, typecheck, docs strict, Lean build, CodeQL) | ✅ strong for research stage |

| Evidence (property tests, bootstrap CIs, reward-hacking detector) | ✅ ahead of most open-source |

| Coverage gate in CI | ⚠️ pytest-cov exists, enforcement unknown |
| API contract (versioned protocol) | ⚠️ #172 not started |

The *sequence* is the only thing to fix: observability → published artifacts → one cloud → protocol seam → native components on the hot path with real numbers. # [EPIC] Release & delivery automation

## Summary

Automate the release pipeline so **every merge produces a versioned, runnable artifact** that downstream work (cloud deployment, enterprise distribution) consumes instead of rebuilding.

Part of the 2026 roadmap decision: release infrastructure lands **before** cloud IaC, so the Azure deployment consumes GHCR images rather than building them in-cluster.

## Motivation

- Current state: manual version tags, docker image built on-demand from source, no coverage signal on PRs.

- Coverage gate protects regression safety during the heavy infrastructure churn that follows.

## Scope

- **R1** — CI: publish multi-arch Docker image to GHCR on tag push
- **R2** — Adopt release-please for semver/tag/changelog automation
- **R3** — Code coverage gate in CI

## Priority

P0 — Start first, parallel with Track E #161 (structured JSON logging).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `ghcr.io/xcoder-es/nomos:vX.Y.Z` exists for every release tag, amd64 + arm64
- [ ] release-please auto-bumps semver from conventional commits, opens release PR, tags and publishes notes on merge
- [ ] CI reports coverage per PR; gate active after 30-day report-only window

## Related

- Depends on: none (foundational)
- Feeds: E2 (one-cloud deployment) — E2-F2 consumes GHCR images
- Tracks with: #161 (JSON logging), Track E #158

## Summary

Deploy Nomos to **one** cloud — Azure — and get it fully green (health, metrics, secrets, smoke) before any multi-cloud work begins. Part of the execution plan approved 2026-08-11: Azure is the reference cloud; AWS and GCP fork this epic's IaC only after Azure is verified.

## Motivation

- The book's provisioning/materialization examples (§A) are Azure-leaning (ACA, ACI, Key Vault) — the docs already point this way.
- One cloud green first = an evidence gate: no parallel triple-IaC design sprawl (execution-plan decision #1).
- Deployment is also the condition that makes the rest of Track E meaningful: OTel, SLOs, and dashboards instrument a *live* system, not a harness.

## Scope

- **A1** — ADR: modular-monolith topology + atomic governance gate
- **A2** — Pulumi IaC: Azure Container Apps deployment (consumes GHCR images from E1)
- **A3** — Deployment verification run (smoke + probe pass + metrics handoff to SLOs)

## Priority

P1 — gated on: #161 (JSON logging, consumed by Log Analytics) and #182 (health endpoints, consumed by ACA probes).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Nomos core + dashboard run in Azure Container Apps from a GHCR artifact
- [ ] healthz/readyz probes pass from ACA (consumes #182 endpoints)

## Summary

Turn the "should we rewrite in Rust/Go?" question into an **evidence-driven decision**. This epic delivers the performance baseline and feasibility studies that decide *whether* native components are justified, and the ADR that keeps the architecture modular-monolith until real signals say otherwise.

- Premature porting is the classic failure mode. The right order: measure → decide → port the smallest justified slice.

Part of epic (E1) — Release & delivery automation. Priority: P0.

## Problem / Motivation

Every version tag today produces no artifact — images are built on demand from source (`Makefile` `docker-build`). The Azure deployment (E2) must consume versioned artifacts, not rebuild them. Also: GitHub-hosted cloud deployment needs a container registry the repo owns.

## Proposed Solution

- New workflow `.github/workflows/publish-image.yml` triggered on `push` of tags `v*`:
  - `docker buildx bake` with `--platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64`
  - Targets: `base` and `with-rl` (matches existing Dockerfile multi-stage README)
  - Push to `ghcr.io/xcoder-es/nomos` (public package)
  - Tags: `vX.Y.Z` (from git tag), `latest` (only for non-pre-release tags)
- Add an OCI `org.opencontainers.image.*` label set (source repo, version, revision)

- [ ] Tagging `vX.Y.Z` publishes `ghcr.io/xcoder-es/nomos:vX.Y.Z` (amd64 + arm64, both targets)

# [Feature]: Adopt release-please for semver/tag/changelog automation

Part of epic (E1) — Release & delivery automation. Priority: P0.

## Problem / Motivation

Versioning is manual: tags cut by hand, version bumps by hand, GitHub releases written by hand. The repo's own convention (atomic commits with conventional prefixes) is exactly what release-please consumes. Every manual cut is toil and an opportunity for inconsistency between `pyproject.toml` version, the git tag, and the release notes.

## Proposed Solution

- Adopt googleapis `release-please-action` v4 with `release-type: python`:
  - Analyzes conventional-commit history; opens a Release PR that bumps `pyproject.toml`, updates CHANGELOG.md, and records a candidate tag
  - On Release PR merge: auto-tag `vX.Y.Z`, auto-publish GitHub release with generated notes, trigger the GHCR publish workflow (E1-R1) via the tag push
- Configure a `.release-please-manifest.json` with initial version matching the current CHANGELOG head
- Document in CONTRIBUTING.md: "semver-relevant changes must use conventional prefixes so release-please can classify them" (the repo already requires this style — now it has a mechanical consumer)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A release PR opens automatically after a `feat:`/`fix:` merge to main
- [ ] Merging the release PR tags vX.Y.Z and publishes a GitHub release with notes
- [ ] GHCR publish workflow fires from the release tag push (E1-R1 integration)
- [ ] CHANGELOG.md stops being hand-edited for new entries (only release-please writes it)

## Alternatives Considered

- Manual tags (status quo): control but toil; rejected by execution-plan decision #2 (2026-08-11).
- semantic-release: works well but shares the repo with nested sub-projects under `gov-budget-proof/`; release-please's manifest model is a better fit for a python root package.
- Custom script: reinventing a well-solved problem.

## Scope

Meta / Project Infrastructure.

## Additional Context

- Decision recorded 2026-08-11: "Adopt release-please for semver/tag/changelog automation (E1-F2)".
- Depends on: repo's existing conventional-commit discipline (AGENTS.md conventions) — already in place.

# [Feature]: Code coverage gate in CI

Part of epic (E1) — Release & delivery automation. Priority: P0.

## Problem / Motivation

The repo has no coverage signal on PRs. The next few quarters bring heavy infrastructure churn (release automation, cloud IaC, packaging) whose regression risk is invisible without a coverage baseline. The harder-review panel's C- grade specifically flagged verification rigor; a coverage gate is the cheap, continuous part of that answer.

## Proposed Solution

- Wire `pytest-cov` into the existing CI pytest job:
  - `coverage run -m pytest` + `coverage report --fail-under=<threshold>`
  - Line threshold proposal: **60%** (baseline at adoption), reviewed upward after 3 months
- Comment coverage delta on PRs (`coverage-action` or comparable) — informational
- 30-day report-only window: CI posts the number, does not fail; after the window the `--fail-under` gate becomes enforced
- Record the baseline number in the issue when the window opens

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] PRs show line + branch coverage comments
- [ ] After the report-only window, CI fails below the threshold
- [ ] Baseline coverage number recorded on this issue
- [ ] `Makefile lint` target and docs mention the coverage command

## Alternatives Considered

- Coverage-driven development on every PR (patch-coverage gating): too strict for a solo-maintainer repo with one LLM reviewer; whole-suite threshold is the right granularity for now.
- No gate: status quo, rejected — the very failure mode the panel flagged.

## Scope

Meta / Project Infrastructure / Testing.

## Additional Context

- Complements Track F hardening (#169 packaging) and the deployment epics: cheap safety net while infra churns.
- pytest is the existing suite; `pytest-cov` is a dev-extra addition only.

# [Feature]: ADR: modular-monolith topology + atomic governance gate Part of epic (E2) — One-cloud deployment: Azure-first. Priority: P1. ## Problem / Motivation Every milestone triggers the same question: *"should we split into microservices now?"* The honest answer is no — the system is one bounded context (the governance gate: Speaker → contracts → identity), and splitting it would break the property the framework actually promises: **the gate is atomic**. There is no existing ADR documenting this, so the decision is re-litigated in every review and risks being overturned by excitement instead of evidence. ## Proposed Solution - New ADR under `docs/adr/` (repo currently has none — establish the convention): - **Decision**: modular monolith. Max two processes in production topology today: core (runner + gRPC/HTTP API when #172 lands) and dashboard (Streamlit). One deployable artifact pair, one data lifetime, one atomic gate. - **Forces**: atomicity of propose→score→veto→vote (Chapter 2), TEE enclave semantics (Appendix A §9 — single enclave), operational simplicity for a solo maintainer. - **Split signals** (when microservices become correct): measured cross-process latency > budget from N1; independent scaling evidence; third-party decoupled consumers facing #172 protocol. - **Topology diagram** (Mermaid, no `
`, per repo convention): core + dashboard + TEE enclave + single ontology backend (Memory or Neo4j). - Reference the ADR from README architecture section and CONTRIBUTING "where things live". ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] `docs/adr/0001-modular-monolith-and-atomic-governance-gate.md` merged, rendered by mkdocs - [ ] Split signals enumerated and tied to specific future issues (N4 supersets this for service-split criteria) - [ ] README architecture section links the ADR ## Alternatives Considered - Event-driven microservices now: breaks gate atomicity, multiplies ops burden 10x for zero measured benefit — rejected in planning (2026-08-11 decision, before any deployment exists). - Monorepo-with-packages only (no ADR): the architecture *decision* stays oral history — this issue exists to fix exactly that. ## Scope Documentation / Meta — architectural decision. ## Additional Context - Feeds: E2-F2 deploys exactly this topology; N4 (E4) extends it with service-split criteria and performance-triggered atomicity.

The Python reference implementation is correct but slow — nobody knows *how* slow, or what the governance gate's latency budget should be. "Rewrite in Rust" and "it's fine as-is" are both claims that need numbers. This issue produces the numbers and the harness that keeps producing them (the evidence gate for N2/N3).

# [Feature]: Feasibility: Rust for TEE-critical runtime (spike + decision doc)

Part of epic (E4) — Native components & performance. Priority: P2. **Gates: N1 numbers + #70 (Lean TEE model).**

## Problem / Motivation

Appendix A's TEE story (single enclave, constant-time enforcement, hardware deadlock breaker) is the framework's strongest security claim — and Python is not credibly enclave-material. The open question: does the *TEE-critical slice* (enclave runtime: hash-chain integrity, constant-time loops, Merkle batching, watchdog) justify a compact Rust core? No porting — prove the cost/benefit first.

## Proposed Solution

- Spike (2-3 focused PRs, no core port):
  1. Map Appendix A §A.9 enclave components to a candidate Rust module surface (small — the slice is < 1k LOC by design)
  2. Benchmark the slice against the N1 hotspots: same operations in Python vs Rust spike (`criterion`-style receipts)
  3. Survey real-TEE options: SGX/SEV-SNP SDK support for Rust (Fortanix/cc-rs), what a future #176 (enterprise TEE integration) would actually run

- [ ] Spike code lives in `spikes/rust-tee-runtime/` (not wired into the core)

- Keep Python + PyPy/compiled-across: to be honest, measure it in the spike alongside Rust.
- WASM sandbox for the gate: a possible middle option — document in the spike if Rust SDK work stalls.

TEE / Security — feasibility research.

- Depends on: N1 (perf evidence), #70 (Lean TEE isolation model — the formal side must stay language-neutral), #172 (protocol defines the gate boundary a native slice would honor).

# [Feature]: ADR: atomicity & service-split criteria

Part of epic (E4) — Native components & performance. Priority: P2.

## Problem / Motivation

A1 (E2) documents the modular-monolith decision for today's topology. This ADR is the *durable* guardrail: the exact, measurable signals that would justify splitting the governance gate into services — so the "no microservices" position cannot be overturned by vibes, only by data.

## Proposed Solution

- `docs/adr/0002-atomic-governance-gate-and-service-split-criteria.md`:
  - **Atomicity as the invariant**: propose→score→veto→vote→commit is one transaction; any split must preserve it (idempotency, fencing, TEE boundary — cite Appendix A §9 and Lean module GovBudgetProof)
  - **Split signals with owners** (each maps to an epic/issue that would produce the data):
    1. Latency: measured cross-process p99 exceeds the N1 budget (owner: E4-N1)
    2. Scaling: one component's resource profile is independently proven (owner: E2-F3 verification metrics)
    3. External decoupling: non-core consumers need only the #172 protocol surface (owner: Track F)
    4. Team/topology: more than one deploy cadence required (owner: ROADMAP review)
  - **Explicit non-signals**: "Rust exists", "Kubernetes is available", "webhooks would be elegant" — each with the reason it does not justify a split
- Link ADR 0002 from ADR 0001 and README; add to mkdocs nav

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] ADR 0002 merged and rendered
- [ ] Every split signal references a concrete owner; non-signals enumerated
- [ ] Cross-referenced both ways with ADR 0001

## Alternatives Considered

- No second ADR (rely on 0001): 0001 is topology-scoped and will age into a historical record; the atomicity invariant deserves its own durable home — this is the framework's core security property, not a topology detail.
- Encode as a proof: Lean #69 proves the invariant inside the gate; the *deployment* decision is organizational and belongs in prose. Belt and suspenders: both exist.

## Scope

Documentation / Meta — architectural decision.

## Additional Context

- This is the "are we crazy?" answer on the board, permanent and cited (execution-plan framing, 2026-08-11).
- Consumed by: commercialization epic #160 reviews, CONTRIBUTING, enterprise tier discussions (#176/#177).

def gh(*args):
    r = subprocess.run(['gh'] + list(args), capture_output=True)

comments = json.loads(gh('api', 'repos/xcoder-es/nomos/pulls/181/comments', '--paginate'))

    out.append('FILE: %s:%s' % (c.get('path'), c.get('line') or c.get('original_line')))
    out.append('AUTHOR: %s (%s)' % (c['user']['login'], c.get('created_at')))
    out.append('BODY:')
    out.append(c.get('body', ''))
    out.append('-' * 60)
with io.open(os.path.join(os.environ['TEMP'], 'opencode', 'pr181_review_comments.txt'), 'w', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
    fh.write('\n'.join(out))
print('%d inline comments' % len(comments))

def _deadlock_check(state: ServerState) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """Return (is_healthy, detail) for the deadlock breaker.

    Fails closed: an unconfigured deadlock breaker is a readiness failure,
    mirroring ``_watchdog_check`` and ``_backend_check``.
    """
    if state.deadlock_breaker is None:
        return False, "deadlock breaker not configured"
    healthy = not state.deadlock_breaker.is_deadlocked
    detail = f"stalled_cycles={state.deadlock_breaker.stalled_cycles}"
    return healthy, detail

# Changelog

All notable changes to the Nomos project are documented here.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.8.0] — 2026-08-11

### Added
- License moved to Apache-2.0 (was CC BY 4.0); LICENSE, README, CLA, and docs references aligned
- Docker build fixed: tests/ and examples/ now copied into the image, base stage is the default build target, .dockerignore added
- MkDocs Material documentation build system (`mkdocs.yml`, `docs/`)
- GitHub Actions workflow to build and deploy docs to GitHub Pages
- GitHub Project #3 for issue tracking with 4 epics (A–D)
- End-to-end pipeline integration test (mini benchmark → analysis → figures → export) (#103)
- Hypothesis property-based tests for contracts (mask merger, enforcement, timelock), Identity Layer (tier rules, multisig thresholds, ontology hashes), and TEE (watchdog, Merkle trees, constant-time ops) (#104)
- Benchmark smoke test job in CI (`benchmark-smoke` in `.github/workflows/tests.yml`) (#105)
- Formal prediction cross-validation harness (#144): 12-prediction confirmation table, adversarial edge-case catalog, sensitivity analysis, and `prove-agent` CLI subcommand
- Auto-refresh toggle for the RL Training tab: polls `results/rl/` every 30s, shows a last-updated timestamp and a "Live from Colab" indicator when new results land (#75)

1: ---
2: title: "Health, readiness, and metrics endpoints"
3: description: "The /healthz, /readyz, and /metrics endpoints exposed by `runner serve`, and how they relate to the TEE watchdog and deadlock breaker."
4: ---
5: 
6: # Server Endpoints
7: 
8: [#server-endpoints](#server-endpoints)
9: 
10: `runner serve` starts a small, read-only HTTP surface for operating the
11: Governance Layer in a long-running process — for example, behind a
12: Kubernetes liveness/readiness probe, or scraped by Prometheus. It is
13: strictly observability: the endpoints below never call
14: `speaker.run_governance_cycle`, and the decision path never imports this
15: module.
16: 
17: ```
18: python -m src.governance.runner serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
19: ```
20: 
21: | Flag | Default | Meaning |
22: | --- | --- | --- |
23: | `--host` | `127.0.0.1` | Bind address |
24: | `--port` | `8000` | Bind port |
25: | `--config` | *(none)* | Path to a `.parliament` config file. Without it, `serve` builds the same example committee used by `runner speaker`. |
26: | `--heartbeat-timeout-ms` | `100.0` | TEE watchdog heartbeat timeout |
27: | `--deadlock-threshold` | `100` | Stalled cycles before the deadlock breaker trips |
28: 
29: ## `GET /healthz` — liveness
30: 
31: [#healthz](#healthz)
32: 
33: Answers one question: *is the process alive and has the parliament
34: configuration been loaded?* This should almost never fail. If it does,
35: the orchestrator should restart the process — the parliament state failed
36: to build and nothing else here can recover that on its own.
37: 
38: ```json
39: {"status": "ok", "parliament_loaded": true, "uptime_s": 12.4}
40: ```
41: 
42: `200` when `parliament_loaded` is `true`, `503` otherwise.
43: 
44: ## `GET /readyz` — readiness
45: 
46: [#readyz](#readyz)
47: 
48: Answers: *should traffic be routed to this process right now?* Unlike
49: `/healthz`, this can flip between `200` and `503` without a restart — it
50: just means "give it a moment." Four checks are reported individually:
51: 
52: - **speaker** — has a `SpeakerStateMachine` been built?
53: - **watchdog** — is the TEE heartbeat watchdog in its `NORMAL` state (not
54:   `HEARTBEAT_MISSED`, `DEADLOCKED`, or `COLD_BOOT`)?
55: - **deadlock_breaker** — has the deadlock breaker *not* tripped (fewer
56:   stalled cycles than its threshold)? This is the "deadlock-breaker
57:   status" the endpoint is required to reflect correctly.
58: - **backend** — does the ontology backend (in-memory or Neo4j) respond to
59:   a `ping()`?
60: 
61: ```json
62: {
63:   "status": "not_ready",
64:   "checks": {
65:     "speaker": {"ok": true, "detail": "ready"},
66:     "watchdog": {"ok": false, "detail": "HEARTBEAT_MISSED"},
67:     "deadlock_breaker": {"ok": true, "detail": "stalled_cycles=0"},
68:     "backend": {"ok": true, "detail": "reachable"}
69:   }
70: }
71: ```
72: 
73: `200` only when every check is `ok`; `503` otherwise, with the failing
74: check(s) visible in the body.
75: 
76: ## `GET /metrics` — Prometheus exposition
77: 
78: [#metrics](#metrics)
79: 
80: Exposes the same signals as `/readyz`, in Prometheus text exposition
81: format, for scraping:
82: 
83: - `governance_parliament_loaded`
84: - `governance_uptime_seconds`
85: - `governance_watchdog_healthy`
86: - `governance_deadlock_stalled_cycles`
87: - `governance_cold_boots_total`
88: - `governance_backend_reachable`
89: 
90: This requires the optional `observability` extra:
91: 
92: ```
93: pip install governance-layer[observability]
94: ```
95: 
96: Without it, `/metrics` returns `503` with a plain-text message pointing
97: to the install command above, instead of crashing the server.
98: 
99: ## Design notes
100: 
101: [#design-notes](#design-notes)
102: 
103: - These endpoints are only mounted by `runner serve` — they are not part
104:   of, and are never imported by, the deterministic decision path in
105:   `speaker.py`.
106: - `serve` doesn't run governance cycles itself, so nothing would
107:   otherwise feed the watchdog a heartbeat. A background thread sends
108:   heartbeats on the same cadence a live decision loop would, so `/readyz`
109:   reflects "the process is alive and responsive." A deployment that runs
110:   decisions in the same process should feed real cycle heartbeats into
111:   the watchdog instead.

def gh(args, data=None):

name: "CodeQL"

on:
  push:
    branches: ["main"]
  pull_request:
    branches: ["main"]
  schedule:
    # Weekly: Sunday 22:00 UTC
    - cron: "0 22 * * 0"

permissions:
  actions: read
  contents: read
  security-events: write

jobs:
  analyze:
    name: Analyze (${{ matrix.language }})
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 360
    permissions:
      actions: read
      contents: read
      security-events: write

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        language: ["python"]

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Initialize CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3
        with:
          languages: ${{ matrix.language }}
          queries: security-extended,security-and-quality

      - name: Autobuild
        uses: github/codeql-action/autobuild@v3

      - name: Perform CodeQL Analysis
        uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3
        with:
          category: "/language:${{ matrix.language }}"

name: "CodeQL"

on:
  push:
    branches: ["main"]
  pull_request:
    branches: ["main"]
  schedule:
    # Weekly deep scan: Sundays 22:25 UTC
    - cron: "25 22 * * 0"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  actions: read
  contents: read
  security-events: write

concurrency:
  # Cancel superseded runs: only the newest analysis per branch/event matters.
  group: "${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.ref }}"
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  # NOTE: this job MUST be named exactly "CodeQL" -- the main ruleset requires a
  # status check with that literal context (produced by default setup before it
  # was disabled). A matrix here would rename the check and re-block every PR.
  CodeQL:
    name: CodeQL
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 360
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        language: ["python"]
    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Initialize CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v4
        with:
          languages: ${{ matrix.language }}
          # Python is interpreted: no build step required, and forcing one can
          # only poison the database (autobuild is a no-op at best).
          build-mode: none
          queries: +security-extended

      - name: Perform CodeQL Analysis
        uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v4
        with:
          category: "/language:${{ matrix.language }}"

  security-and-quality:
    name: Analyze (${{ matrix.language }}, security-and-quality)
    # Deep sweep: the full default + extended + quality suite, weekly and on
    # manual dispatch. Not required by the ruleset; it complements the
    # per-PR security-extended pass above.
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule' || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 360
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        language: ["python"]
    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Initialize CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v4
        with:
          languages: ${{ matrix.language }}
          build-mode: none
          queries: +security-extended,security-and-quality

      - name: Perform CodeQL Analysis
        uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v4
        with:
          category: "/language:${{ matrix.language }}/deep"

131:         ]

133:     def _apply_budgets(self, proposals: list[Proposal]) -> list[Proposal]:
134:         """Enforce per-member proposal budgets (κ₂).
135: 
136:         Filters proposals so that no member exceeds their ``budget``
137:         in a single cycle. This prevents SDoS attacks where a single
138:         member floods the agenda.
139: 
140:         Args:
141:             proposals: Raw proposals from all members.
142: 
143:         Returns:
144:             Filtered list respecting per-member budgets.
145:         """
146:         budgets = defaultdict(int)
147:         filtered = []
148:         for p in proposals:
149:             member = self.members.get(p.member_id)
150:             if member is None:
151:                 continue
152:             if budgets[p.member_id] < member.budget:
153:                 filtered.append(p)
154:                 budgets[p.member_id] += 1
155:         return filtered
156: 
157:     def _sort_agenda(self, proposals: list[Proposal]) -> list[Proposal]:
158:         """Sort proposals by priority tag, then by submission time.
159: 
160:         Lower tag values (higher urgency) appear first. Within the same
161:         tag, earlier timestamps win. This is the priority-sorting
162:         procedure from Ch2 §2.3.
163: 
164:         Args:
165:             proposals: Budget-filtered proposals.
166: 
167:         Returns:
168:             Sorted list.
169:         """
170:         return sorted(proposals, key=lambda p: (p.tag, p.timestamp))
171: 
172:     def set_agenda(self, proposals: list[Proposal]) -> list[Proposal]:
173:         """Build the ordered agenda: apply budgets, then sort.
174: 
175:         This is the public entry point for agenda creation, called
176:         at the start of each governance cycle.
177: 
178:         Args:
179:             proposals: Raw proposals from Parliament members.
180: 
181:         Returns:
182:             Priority-ordered, budget-respecting agenda.
183:         """
184:         return self._sort_agenda(self._apply_budgets(proposals))

190:         that need per-member scores without running a full governance
191:         cycle. The governance cycle itself scores proposals internally;
192:         this method exposes the same evaluation deterministically.
193:

197:

200:         """

202: 
203:     def _score_proposal(self, state: Any, proposal: Proposal) -> dict[str, float]:

208:             The ratings are collected by the Speaker's office before

221:         return scores

224:         self, proposals: list[Proposal], integrity_scores: dict[str, float]

227: 
228:         If a member's Integrity score falls below
229:         ``TAG_COMPLIANCE_THRESHOLD``, the member is flagged. After
230:         ``FALSIFICATION_BUDGET_CUTOFF`` flags, their proposal budget
231:         is halved (minimum 1).

234:         from persistently submitting mis-tagged proposals to game the
235:         agenda ordering (Ch2 §2.4.2).

239:             integrity_scores: Map of member_id → Integrity score.
240: 
241:         Returns:

243:         """

246:             if score < self.TAG_COMPLIANCE_THRESHOLD:

249:                 )

251:             if count >= self.FALSIFICATION_BUDGET_CUTOFF:

261:         falls below the member's ``veto_threshold``.
262:

264:         regardless of the member's weight. This gives Safety and
265:         Integrity effective blocking power despite being a minority

273:             Empty list means no veto — proceed to voting.
274:         """

277:             if scores.get(member_id, 0.0) < member.veto_threshold:
278:                 vetoers.append(member_id)
279:         return vetoers

282:         """Perform weighted range voting.
283: 
284:         The weighted average is computed as:
285: 
286:         .. math::
287: 
288:             \\text{score} = \\frac{\\sum_i w_i \\cdot V_i(s, a)}{\\sum_i w_i}
289: 
290:         The threshold depends on the decision class:
291: 
292:         ================ ========= ====================================
293:         Decision class   Threshold Notes
294:         ================ ========= ====================================
295:         ``"routine"``    0.50      Simple majority
296:         ``"high_impact"`` 0.66     Supermajority (contract enact/revoke)
297:         ``"identity"``   1.0       Unanimity (core commitment changes)
298:         ================ ========= ====================================
299: 
300:         Args:
301:             scores: Map of member_id → evaluation scores.
302:             decision_class: One of ``"routine"``, ``"high_impact"``,
303:                 or ``"identity"``.
304: 
305:         Returns:
306:             True if the weighted average meets or exceeds the threshold.
307:         """
308:         total_weight = 0.0
309:         weighted_sum = 0.0
310:         for member_id, member in self.members.items():
311:             w = member.weight
312:             s = scores.get(member_id, 0.0)
313:             weighted_sum += w * s
314:             total_weight += w
315:         if total_weight == 0.0:
316:             return False
317:         avg_score = weighted_sum / total_weight
318:         if decision_class == "identity":
319:             threshold = 1.0
320:         elif decision_class == "high_impact":
321:             threshold = self.supermajority_threshold
322:         else:
323:             threshold = self.majority_threshold
324:         return avg_score >= threshold

326:     def run_governance_cycle(
327:         self,
328:         state: Any,
329:         raw_proposals: list[Proposal],

336:         1. Filters proposals by budget (κ₂)
337:         2. Orders the agenda by priority + timestamp
338:         3. In round 0, checks tag compliance (falsification detection)
339:         4. For each proposal in order:

341:            b. Checks for vetoes — if any, skip to next proposal

345:         Args:
346:             state: Current environment state (passed to each member's
347:                 ``evaluate_proposal``).
348:             raw_proposals: All proposals submitted by members.
349:             decision_class: Determines voting threshold (see
350:                 :meth:`_resolve_vote`).

352:         Returns:
353:             A :class:`GovernanceDecision` containing the winning action,
354:             scores, vetoes, and metadata (including falsification counts).
355:         """
356:         self._falsification_counts = {}
357:         agenda = self.set_agenda(raw_proposals)
358: 
359:         for _round in range(self.max_rounds):
360:             if _round == 0:
361:                 integrity_scores = {}
362:                 for p in agenda:
363:                     p_scores = self._score_proposal(state, p)
364:                     integrity_scores[p.member_id] = p_scores.get("integrity", 1.0)
365:                 self._check_tag_compliance(agenda, integrity_scores)

381:                         },
382:                     )

389:                 "reason": f"No consensus after {self.max_rounds} rounds",

"""
Structured JSON logging for the Nomos core — standard library only (#161).

Design goals (matching ``#161``):

- **Zero dependencies:** built on :mod:`logging` + :mod:`json` only. The
  algorithmic core stays dependency-free and deterministic.
- **Stable schema:** every record serializes to the same key order:
  ``timestamp``, ``level``, ``logger``, ``message``, then sorted structured
  extras, then ``exception`` (if any).
- **Deterministic:** timestamps are ISO-8601 UTC (``Z`` suffix), key order is
  fixed, and non-JSON-native values are coerced with ``str()`` — the same
  inputs always produce byte-identical log lines. Logging never feeds back
  into decision logic (see the determinism test in ``tests/test_observability.py``).
- **Secret redaction:** values under sensitive key names (API keys, tokens,
  passwords, private keys, authorization headers) and well-known secret
  shapes (OpenAI ``sk-...`` keys, ``Bearer`` tokens, AWS ``AKIA...`` keys,
  PEM private key blocks) are replaced with ``[REDACTED]`` everywhere in the
  output — message text, structured extras, and exception traces alike.
- **Two output modes:** compact JSON (one object per line — production/SIEM)
  and indented JSON (local debugging).

Usage::

    from nomos.observability import configure_logging

    configure_logging(fmt="json", level=logging.INFO)

    logger = logging.getLogger("nomos.speaker")
    logger.info("governance_decision", extra={"phase": "decision", "action": "shutdown"})

Output::

    {"timestamp": "2026-08-11T15:04:05.123Z", "level": "INFO", "logger": "nomos.speaker",
     "message": "governance_decision", "action": "shutdown", "phase": "decision"}
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as _dt
import json
import logging
import math
import re
import sys
from typing import Any

__all__ = [
    "JsonFormatter",
    "RESERVED_EXTRA_KEYS",
    "configure_logging",
]


_RESERVED_EXTRA_KEYS = frozenset(
    {
        "timestamp",
        "level",
        "logger",
        "message",
        "exception",
    }
)
"""Key names the formatter owns; structured extras may never collide with them."""

RESERVED_EXTRA_KEYS = _RESERVED_EXTRA_KEYS
"""Public alias so callers can strip colliding keys before passing ``extra``."""

_STANDARD_RECORD_ATTRS = frozenset(
    {
        "name",
        "msg",
        "args",
        "levelname",
        "levelno",
        "pathname",
        "filename",
        "module",
        "exc_info",
        "exc_text",
        "stack_info",
        "lineno",
        "funcName",
        "created",
        "msecs",
        "relativeCreated",
        "thread",
        "threadName",
        "processName",
        "process",
        "taskName",
        "message",
    }
)
"""Structured extras are everything else in ``record.__dict__`` (and no more)."""

_SECRET_KEY_RE = re.compile(
    r"(?i).*(api[_-]?key|secret|passw(ord|d)?|pwd|token|private[_-]?key|"
    r"authorization|credential|bearer|access[_-]?key|signing[_-]?key|"
    r"session[_-]?id).*"
)
"""Key-name based redaction: any key containing one of these words is redacted."""

_SECRET_VALUE_PATTERNS = (
    # OpenAI-style API keys: sk-abcdef...
    re.compile(r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}"),
    # Bearer tokens in header values / messages.
    re.compile(r"Bearer[ \t]+[A-Za-z0-9._~+/-]{10,}"),
    # AWS access key IDs.
    re.compile(r"AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}"),
    # PEM private key blocks (multi-line, any key type).
    re.compile(
        r"-----BEGIN [A-Z0-9 ]*PRIVATE KEY-----.*?-----END [A-Z0-9 ]*PRIVATE KEY-----",
        re.DOTALL,
    ),
)
"""Value-shape based redaction applied to every string in the output."""

_REDACTED = "[REDACTED]"


def _redact_string(text: str) -> str:
    """Replace known secret shapes inside ``text`` with ``[REDACTED]``."""
    redacted = text
    for pattern in _SECRET_VALUE_PATTERNS:
        redacted = pattern.sub(_REDACTED, redacted)
    return redacted


def _redact_value(value: Any, key: str = "") -> Any:
    """Recursively redact ``value``; ``key`` triggers name-based redaction.

    The return value keeps the exact structural shape (dict/list scalars) so
    the log line stays parseable JSON.
    """
    if _SECRET_KEY_RE.match(key):
        return _REDACTED
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return {k: _redact_value(v, str(k)) for k, v in value.items()}
    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
        return [_redact_value(v, "") for v in value]
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return _redact_string(value)
    return value


def _safe(value: Any) -> Any:
    """Coerce ``value`` to a strictly JSON-serializable form.

    Only native JSON scalars/containers are kept as-is; everything else is
    converted deterministically via ``str()`` (datetimes become ISO-8601,
    non-finite floats become strings, custom objects become their repr).
    """
    if value is None or isinstance(value, (str, bool)):
        return value
    if isinstance(value, int):
        return value
    if isinstance(value, float):
        return value if math.isfinite(value) else str(value)
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return {str(k): _safe(v) for k, v in value.items()}
    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
        return [_safe(v) for v in value]
    if isinstance(value, (_dt.datetime, _dt.date)):
        return value.isoformat()
    if isinstance(value, (set, frozenset)):
        return [_safe(v) for v in sorted(value, key=repr)]
    return str(value)


def _iso_utc_now() -> str:
    """Current time as ISO-8601 UTC with millisecond precision (``Z`` suffix)."""
    now = _dt.datetime.now(_dt.timezone.utc)
    return now.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f")[:-3] + "Z"


class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    """Emit one deterministic JSON object per log record.

    Schema (fixed key order)::

        timestamp  ISO-8601 UTC, e.g. 2026-08-11T15:04:05.123Z
        level      record levelname (e.g. INFO)
        logger     record logger name (e.g. nomos.speaker)
        message    the formatted log message
        ...        every structured extra, sorted alphabetically
        exception  traceback text, only when an exception is attached

    Secrets are redacted at formatting time (both message text and nested
    structured values), so nothing sensitive reaches the output even if a
    caller forgets to scrub its own data.
    """

    def __init__(self, pretty: bool = False):
        """Args:
            pretty: indent the JSON with two spaces instead of one line.
        """
        super().__init__()
        self.pretty = pretty

    @staticmethod
    def _extra_fields(record: logging.LogRecord) -> dict[str, Any]:
        extras = {
            k: v
            for k, v in record.__dict__.items()
            if k not in _STANDARD_RECORD_ATTRS and k not in _RESERVED_EXTRA_KEYS
        }
        return {k: extras[k] for k in sorted(extras)}

    @staticmethod
    def _exception_text(record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        if record.exc_info:
            return _redact_string(
                "".join(
                    __import__("traceback").format_exception(*record.exc_info)
                ).rstrip()
            )
        if record.exc_text:
            return _redact_string(record.exc_text)
        return ""

    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        payload: dict[str, Any] = {
            "timestamp": _iso_utc_now(),
            "level": record.levelname,
            "logger": record.name,
            "message": record.getMessage(),
        }
        payload.update(self._extra_fields(record))
        exception = self._exception_text(record)
        if exception:
            payload["exception"] = exception

        redacted = _redact_value(_safe(payload))

        if self.pretty:
            return json.dumps(redacted, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
        return json.dumps(redacted, ensure_ascii=False)


class _PlainFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    """Human-readable one-liner for local development (no JSON)."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__("%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")


_FORMATS = {
    "json": JsonFormatter(pretty=False),
    "json-pretty": JsonFormatter(pretty=True),
    "plain": _PlainFormatter(),
}

_LOG_LEVELS = {
    "DEBUG": logging.DEBUG,
    "INFO": logging.INFO,
    "WARNING": logging.WARNING,
    "ERROR": logging.ERROR,
}


def configure_logging(
    fmt: str = "plain",
    level: str | int = logging.INFO,
    logger_names: tuple[str, ...] = ("nomos",),
) -> None:
    """Install the Nomos log handler on the given logger names (stdlib only).

    Args:
        fmt: One of ``"plain"`` (local dev), ``"json"`` (one object per
            line, production/SIEM), or ``"json-pretty"`` (indented JSON).
        level: Logging level: ``"DEBUG"``/``"INFO"``/``"WARNING"``/``"ERROR"``
            or a numeric ``logging`` constant.
        logger_names: Logger names to propagate through (default: only
            ``nomos`` — third-party loggers are left untouched).

    Returns:
        None. Idempotent: repeated calls replace the previous Nomos handler
        instead of stacking duplicates.
    """
    if isinstance(level, str):
        level = _LOG_LEVELS[level.upper()]
    if fmt not in _FORMATS:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown log format {fmt!r}; choose from {sorted(_FORMATS)}")

    handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stderr)
    handler.setFormatter(_FORMATS[fmt])
    handler.setLevel(level)

    for name in logger_names:
        logger = logging.getLogger(name)
        logger.setLevel(level)
        for existing in list(logger.handlers):
            if getattr(existing, "_nomos_handler", False):
                logger.removeHandler(existing)
        handler._nomos_handler = True  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
        logger.addHandler(handler)
        logger.propagate = True

No single platform — the observability stack (epic #158) is **vendor-neutral and layered**, structured logging is just F1 of 8:

| Layer | Standard | Where it lands |

| Logs | JSON, ISO-8601 UTC, one object/line | #161 (in progress) → SIEM-ready |

| Alerting | Prometheus recording rules + **Alertmanager** YAML, SLO error-budget math | #165 |
| Dashboards | **Grafana** dashboard JSON, validated in CI | #168 |
| Viewing | Streamlit trace viewer + OTLP JSON import/export | #166 |
| CI | In-repo OTLP collector smoke (no external services) | #167 |

So: OTLP + Prometheus/Alertmanager/Grafana as the wallet — and Track J (Azure-first deployment) consumes it with Azure Monitor Managed Prometheus/Grafana, no vendor lock-in. Plus the tamper-evident audit chain which is the framework-specific tier. Up next after #161: #162 (OTel), #164 (audit) per the deploy-first order.

import io
import json
import logging
import subprocess
import sys

import pytest

from src.nomos.observability import configure_logging
from src.nomos.speaker import SpeakerStateMachine

from .test_speaker import _make_proposal

from src.nomos.committee.members import ExampleRewardMember, ExampleSafetyMember


def _capture(fmt: str = "plain", level: str = "info"):
    """Configure logging and return (logger, StringIO capturing its output)."""
    configure_logging(fmt=fmt, level=level)
    logger = logging.getLogger("nomos")
    buf = io.StringIO()
    handler = logging.StreamHandler(buf)
    handler.setFormatter(logging.getLogger("nomos").handlers[0].formatter)
    logger.addHandler(handler)
    logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
    return logger, buf


def _parse_json_lines(buf):
    return [json.loads(line) for line in buf.getvalue().splitlines() if line.strip()]


class TestConfigureLogging:
    def test_plain_default(self):
        logger, buf = _capture()
        logger.info("hello", extra={"event": "ping"})
        line = buf.getvalue().strip()
        assert line == "hello"
        assert "event" not in line

    def test_json_format(self):
        logger, buf = _capture(fmt="json")
        logger.info("hello", extra={"event": "ping", "n": 7})
        records = _parse_json_lines(buf)
        assert len(records) == 1
        rec = records[0]
        assert rec["message"] == "hello"
        assert rec["event"] == "ping"
        assert rec["n"] == 7
        assert rec["level"] == "INFO"
        assert "timestamp" in rec
        assert "logger" in rec

    def test_json_pretty_format(self):
        logger, buf = _capture(fmt="json-pretty")
        logger.info("hi", extra={"event": "x"})
        assert "\n" in buf.getvalue().strip()
        records = _parse_json_lines(buf)
        assert records[0]["message"] == "hi"

    def test_level_debug(self):
        logger, buf = _capture(fmt="json", level="debug")
        logger.debug("dbg", extra={"event": "d"})
        logger.info("inf", extra={"event": "i"})
        assert any(r["message"] == "dbg" for r in _parse_json_lines(buf))
        assert any(r["message"] == "inf" for r in _parse_json_lines(buf))

    def test_level_info_suppresses_debug(self):
        logger, buf = _capture(fmt="json", level="info")
        logger.debug("dbg", extra={"event": "d"})
        assert _parse_json_lines(buf) == []

    def test_plain_json_roundtrip_valid(self):
        logger, buf = _capture(fmt="json")
        for i in range(3):
            logger.info("msg", extra={"event": "tick", "i": i})
        records = _parse_json_lines(buf)
        assert [r["i"] for r in records] == [0, 1, 2]


class TestSpeakerTelemetry:
    def _speaker(self):
        return SpeakerStateMachine(
            members={"reward": ExampleRewardMember(), "safety": ExampleSafetyMember()},
            default_action="shutdown",
        )

    def test_cycle_emits_decision_event(self):
        _, buf = _capture(fmt="json", level="info")
        speaker = self._speaker()
        proposal = _make_proposal("reward")
        speaker.run_governance_cycle(state="normal", raw_proposals=[proposal])
        records = _parse_json_lines(buf)
        events = [r["event"] for r in records]
        assert "governance_cycle_start" in events
        assert "governance_decision" in events

    def test_decision_has_action_and_round(self):
        _, buf = _capture(fmt="json", level="info")
        speaker = self._speaker()
        proposal = _make_proposal("reward")
        decision = speaker.run_governance_cycle(
            state="normal", raw_proposals=[proposal]
        )
        records = _parse_json_lines(buf)
        decision_rec = [r for r in records if r["event"] == "governance_decision"][0]
        assert decision_rec["action"] == decision.action
        assert decision_rec["round"] == 1
        assert decision_rec["is_default"] is False
        assert "falsification_counts" in decision_rec

    def test_extra_context_included(self):
        _, buf = _capture(fmt="json", level="info")
        speaker = self._speaker()
        from src.nomos.models import PriorityTag

        proposal = _make_proposal("reward", tag=PriorityTag.ROUTINE)
        speaker.run_governance_cycle(
            state="normal",
            raw_proposals=[proposal],
            extra_context={"strategy": "pipeline_test", "run_id": "abc-123"},
        )
        records = _parse_json_lines(buf)
        assert all(r.get("strategy") == "pipeline_test" for r in records)
        assert all(r.get("run_id") == "abc-123" for r in records)

    def test_extra_context_never_changes_decision(self):
        _, buf = _capture(fmt="json", level="info")
        speaker = self._speaker()
        proposal = _make_proposal("reward")
        d1 = speaker.run_governance_cycle(
            state="normal", raw_proposals=[proposal]
        )
        d2 = speaker.run_governance_cycle(
            state="normal",
            raw_proposals=[proposal],
            extra_context={"strategy": "evil", "phase": "hack"},
        )
        assert d1.action == d2.action
        assert d1.scores == d2.scores

Honest answer after re-reading `observability.py` end-to-end:

**It's neither — it's the standard logger-hierarchy convention, which is the right middle ground.** How new modules plug in:

```python
logger = logging.getLogger("nomos.new_module")   # ONE line — nothing else needed
logger.info("event_name", extra={"action": x, "phase": y})  # the event schema
```

That's the entire integration surface:
- `configure_logging()` installs on the `"nomos"` ancestor only (observability.py:289-296); every child logger (`nomos.speaker`, `nomos.foo`) inherits the JSON formatter, secret redaction, `_safe()` coercion, and level for free via propagation.
- New modules never import `observability` at all — they just follow the `extra={}` convention.
- Format switching (`plain` → `json` → `json-pretty`) is a one-call change, applied globally — nothing per-module.

**What's NOT there yet (honest gaps):**
1. No decorator API — `@observe(event=...)` doesn't exist yet; I held off because it's premature until the #162/#166 OTel ingestion shapes the trace-side API. The `extra=` convention is the schema contract today.
2. No context propagation — `run_id`/`strategy` must be threaded manually via `extra_context` (contextvars-based propagation is the natural next step, again best done at OTel time).
3. `logger_names` param means third-party loggers (neo4j driver, openai SDK) stay untouched unless explicitly opted in — deliberate, keeps the core leak-free.

One real wart to fix now: it's **two** abstractions of "abstract" — `RESERVED_EXTRA_KEYS` both here and in speaker. Verifying no drift

def _capture(fmt: str = "plain", level: str = "info"):
    """Configure logging redirected to a StringIO and return (logger, buf).

    ``configure_logging`` binds its own ``StreamHandler(sys.stderr)`` at
    construction time, so swapping ``sys.stderr`` before configuring makes the
    emitted lines land in ``buf`` — no handler copying, no shared-state leaks.
    """
    buf = io.StringIO()
    real_stderr = sys.stderr
    sys.stderr = buf
    try:
        configure_logging(fmt=fmt, level=level)
        logger = logging.getLogger("nomos")
        return logger, buf
    finally:
        sys.stderr = real_stderr

## Description
Structured JSON logging foundation for the Governance Layer — first slice of the Track E observability epic (#158 F1). Fixes #161. The algorithmic core stays **zero-dependency and fully deterministic**; logging never feeds back into decision logic (covered by a dedicated test).

- **`nomos.observability`** (stdlib only — no new dependencies):
  - `configure_logging(fmt=, level=)` → `plain` / `json` (one object per line, SIEM-ready) / `json-pretty`; idempotent install on the `nomos` logger tree.
  - Deterministic schema: `timestamp` (ISO-8601 UTC), `level`, `logger`, `message`, alphabetically-sorted structured extras.
  - Recursive secret redaction: key-name based (api_key, token, password, authorization, ...) + value-shape based (OpenAI `sk-`, Bearer, AWS `AKIA`, PEM blocks) — applied to messages, extras, and exception traces.
  - `_safe()` coercion so any object serializes deterministically (datetimes → ISO, non-finite floats → strings, sets → sorted lists).
- **Speaker telemetry**: emits `governance_cycle_start`, `proposal_scored`, `proposal_vetoed`, `governance_decision` events. New `run_governance_cycle(extra_context=...)` threads call-site context (strategy, run_id, ...) into every record — strictly observational, never influences the decision.
- **CLI**: `--log-format` / `--log-level` global flags on every runner subcommand; the `all` benchmark command emits one `benchmark_run` JSON line per strategy-scenario/seed (reward, deadlocks, violations).
- Tests: `tests/test_observability.py` — 12 tests across formats, levels, telemetry event presence, extra-context isolation, CLI integration.

## Type of Change
- [ ] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to not work as expected)
- [ ] Documentation update (book, README, API docs)
- [ ] Refactor / cleanup (no functional change)
- [ ] Formal verification (Lean proofs, predictions)

## Checklist
- [x] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md) guidelines
- [x] My code follows the project's style guidelines (type hints, no comments in code, docstrings for public APIs)
- [x] I have performed a self-review of my code
- [x] I have added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works
- [x] New and existing unit tests pass locally (`python -m pytest tests/ -v`)
- [ ] I have run the benchmark suite if this affects experiments (`python -m src.nomos.runner all --baselines`) — not run; full regression suite (811 tests) passes and no experiment logic changed
- [x] I have run the formal prediction suite if this affects core logic (`python -m src.nomos.runner prove --all`) — no core decision semantics changed; logging is observational (test-proven)
- [x] I have made corresponding changes to the documentation (book chapters, README, docstrings)
- [x] My changes generate no new warnings
- [x] I have updated the [CHANGELOG.md](../CHANGELOG.md) if this is a user-facing change

## Testing
- `python -m pytest tests/ -q` → **811 passed** (locally, full suite)
- `ruff format --check src/` + `ruff check` clean after formatting fixes
- Manual exercise: `python -m src.nomos.runner --log-format json speaker` produces valid NDJSON with structured events (verified on Windows PowerShell 5.1)

## Screenshots / Output
Example output of the structured JSON mode:
```
{"timestamp": "2026-08-11T15:55:37.826Z", "level": "INFO", "logger": "nomos.speaker", "message": "governance_decision", "action": "safe_middle_road", "event": "governance_decision", "falsification_counts": {"reward": 1}, "is_default": false, "phase": "decision", "round": 1, "winning_proposal": "<Proposal by safety tag=CRITICAL_SAFETY>"}
```

## Additional Notes
- Layering with the rest of Track E: this establishes the structured event contract; #162/#166 will add OpenTelemetry export and context propagation on top of the same formatter.
- New modules need only `logging.getLogger("nomos.<module>")` + the `extra={...}` event convention — no observability import required; formatting/redaction/coercion are inherited via the logger tree.
